difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY because it tests a single concept (every edge must point forward in a topological order), and each of the four orderings is accepted or rejected by a quick scan of the six edges, in about 1–1.5 minutes.
stem:
Consider the directed acyclic graph (DAG) below:

![Figure: A DAG with seven vertices. P and R each have an edge into Q. Q has edges to S and to V. S has an edge to U, and V has an edge to T.](/pyq/2024/fig/Q51-1.png)

Which of the following is/are valid vertex orderings that can be obtained from a topological sort of the DAG?

options.label: A
options.text: P Q R S T U V

options.label: B
options.text: P R Q V S U T

options.label: C
options.text: P Q R S V U T

options.label: D
options.text: P R Q S V T U

solution.quick: The edges are $P \to Q$, $R \to Q$, $Q \to S$, $Q \to V$, $S \to U$ and $V \to T$. In a topological order every edge must point forward. So $Q$ must come after **both** $P$ and $R$, and $U$ after $S$, and $T$ after $V$. (A) and (C) place $Q$ before $R$, and (A) also places $T$ before $V$, so both are invalid. (B) and (D) respect all six edges. Answer: **(B), (D)**.

steps.title: Read the edges from the figure
steps.body:
The DAG has 7 vertices and 6 directed edges:

$$P \to Q,\quad R \to Q,\quad Q \to S,\quad Q \to V,\quad S \to U,\quad V \to T$$

In-degrees: $P = 0$, $R = 0$, $Q = 2$, $S = 1$, $V = 1$, $U = 1$, $T = 1$. The only sources (in-degree 0) are $P$ and $R$.

steps.title: The rule for a topological order
steps.body:
A topological order is an arrangement of **all** vertices in a line such that for every edge $u \to v$, $u$ appears before $v$. So a given sequence is valid exactly when none of the six edges points backwards. The edges give these precedence constraints:

- $P$ before $Q$ and $R$ before $Q$. Because $Q$ has two parents, it cannot appear until both $P$ and $R$ have appeared.
- $Q$ before $S$ and $Q$ before $V$.
- $S$ before $U$.
- $V$ before $T$.

steps.title: Check each ordering edge by edge
steps.body:
Positions are numbered 1 to 7 from the left.

| Option | Ordering | $P, R$ before $Q$? | $Q$ before $S, V$? | $S$ before $U$? | $V$ before $T$? | Valid? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (A) | P Q R S T U V | No: $Q$ is 2nd, $R$ is 3rd | Yes | Yes (4th, 6th) | No: $T$ is 5th, $V$ is 7th | **No** |
| (B) | P R Q V S U T | Yes (1st, 2nd, then $Q$ 3rd) | Yes | Yes (5th, 6th) | Yes (4th, 7th) | **Yes** |
| (C) | P Q R S V U T | No: $Q$ is 2nd, $R$ is 3rd | Yes | Yes (4th, 6th) | Yes (5th, 7th) | **No** |
| (D) | P R Q S V T U | Yes (1st, 2nd, then $Q$ 3rd) | Yes | Yes (4th, 7th) | Yes (5th, 6th) | **Yes** |

(A) violates $R \to Q$ and $V \to T$. (C) violates $R \to Q$. (B) and (D) violate nothing.

steps.title: Confirm (B) and (D) with Kahn's algorithm
steps.body:
Kahn's algorithm repeatedly outputs any vertex whose in-degree has dropped to 0 (the **ready** set), then decrements the in-degrees of its successors. A sequence is a topological order exactly when every vertex is ready at the moment it is output.

**(B) P R Q V S U T.** Ready $\{P, R\}$. Output $P$, so $Q$ has in-degree 1 and the ready set is $\{R\}$. Output $R$, so $Q$ drops to 0 and the ready set is $\{Q\}$. Output $Q$: ready $\{S, V\}$. Output $V$: ready $\{S, T\}$. Output $S$: ready $\{T, U\}$. Output $U$: ready $\{T\}$. Output $T$. Every vertex was ready when chosen, so (B) is valid.

**(D) P R Q S V T U.** The first three steps are the same, leaving ready $\{S, V\}$. Output $S$: ready $\{V, U\}$. Output $V$: ready $\{U, T\}$. Output $T$: ready $\{U\}$. Output $U$. So (D) is valid.

**(A) and (C)** both fail at the second position. After $P$ is output, $Q$ still has in-degree 1 because it is waiting for $R$, so $Q$ is not ready.

steps.title: How many valid orders exist (sanity check)
steps.body: The first three positions must be $P, R$ in either order and then $Q$: 2 ways. After $Q$, the chains $S \to U$ and $V \to T$ are independent. Any interleaving of the two 2-vertex chains keeps the order within each chain, and there are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ such interleavings. That gives $2 \times 6 = 12$ valid topological orders; a brute-force check over all $7! = 5040$ permutations also finds 12. (B) and (D) are two of them.

solution.teaching:
**What a topological order is.** A directed acyclic graph (DAG) encodes "must happen before" constraints, such as course prerequisites or build dependencies. A *topological order* lists **all** the vertices in a line so that every edge $u \to v$ points forward: $u$ comes before $v$. Such an order exists exactly when the graph has no directed cycle. It is usually **not unique**: if no directed path joins two vertices, either may come first.

**Kahn's algorithm (queue based).** Compute every vertex's in-degree and put the in-degree-0 vertices in a ready set. Repeatedly remove any ready vertex, output it, and decrement the in-degree of each of its successors. A successor whose in-degree reaches 0 becomes ready. Every choice from the ready set leads to a valid order, and every valid order can be produced by some sequence of choices. The running time is $O(V + E)$.

**DFS-based method.** Run depth-first search and record each vertex when it *finishes*, that is, after all its descendants are done. The **reverse** of this finishing order is a topological order. The *discovery* (pre-order) sequence of DFS is **not** in general a topological order.

**Checking a proposed order** is even easier. Record each vertex's position and verify, for every edge $u \to v$, that $\text{pos}(u) < \text{pos}(v)$.

**Back to this question.** The key vertex is $Q$, which has in-degree 2. Neither $P$ nor $R$ alone releases it, so the first three places must be $\{P, R\}$ in some order, followed by $Q$. Options (A) and (C) put $Q$ second, so they fail immediately. After $Q$, the two chains $S \to U$ and $V \to T$ may interleave freely as long as each chain keeps its own order. (B) and (D) are two such interleavings.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: $Q$ (2nd) appears before its parent $R$ (3rd), which violates $R \to Q$. $T$ (5th) also appears before its parent $V$ (7th), which violates $V \to T$. Not a topological order.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: $P, R$ come first, then $Q$. $V$ (4th) precedes $T$ (7th), and $S$ (5th) precedes $U$ (6th). All six edges point forward, and Kahn's algorithm can produce this sequence.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: The tail $S, V, U, T$ is fine, but $Q$ (2nd) precedes $R$ (3rd), which violates the edge $R \to Q$. $Q$ cannot be output while one of its parents is still pending.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: $P, R$, then $Q$. After that, $S$ (4th) is before $U$ (7th) and $V$ (5th) is before $T$ (6th). Every edge points forward, so this is a valid topological order.

solution.shortcut: Only vertices with several parents, or chains, constrain the order. Here $Q$ has two parents, so the prefix must be $\{P, R\}$ followed by $Q$. That rules out (A) and (C) at a glance. For the rest, just check $S$ before $U$ and $V$ before $T$.
solution.commonTrap: Writing down the DFS discovery order from $P$ (P, Q, S, U, …) and treating it as a topological sort. $Q$ cannot be output until **both** of its parents, $P$ and $R$, have been output. Discovery order is not a topological order; the reverse of the DFS *finishing* order is.

transcription.notes: Transcribed from the official paper rendering and independently checked against it. The DAG is the raster image embedded in the official PDF (page 33), copied unchanged as Q51-1.png; it carries faint traces of the 'GATE 2024' watermark. The figure file was re-inspected: its edges are P→Q, R→Q, Q→S, Q→V, S→U and V→T, as in the official crop. The stem wording and the four option orderings match the official crop and the PDF text layer letter by letter.

answerVerification.method: Blind independent re-solve + Python check agrees with official key
answerVerification.notes: Independent verifier solved it blind from the official crop before seeing the key. Reading the edges P→Q, R→Q, Q→S, Q→V, S→U and V→T, (A) violates R→Q and V→T, (C) violates R→Q, and (B) and (D) respect every edge, giving B;D. The stored Python check tests every edge against each ordering and brute-forces all 5040 permutations; it finds 12 topological orders, matching 2 × C(4,2). This matches the official key B;D.
